kernelIdea: A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets. The step splits subsets by whether they contain a chosen element, each group matching the subsets of a set with one fewer element.

kernels.l1: Two toys make four different bags. Every new toy doubles it.
kernels.l2: Count the different bags you could pack. With one toy there are two, with two toys four, with three toys eight. Each new toy doubles the count, because it is either in the bag or out.
kernels.l3: A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets. Each new element doubles the number, because every subset either contains it or does not — and the domino argument turns that observation into a proof.
kernels.l4: A set with n elements has exactly 2ⁿ subsets. The inductive step fixes one element and splits the subsets into those containing it and those not; each group matches the subsets of the remaining n−1 elements, and the two halves add to the next power of two.
kernels.l5: A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets. One proof is by induction, splitting the subsets by whether they contain a chosen element; another counts one yes-or-no choice per element. Having two proofs of the same result is normal, and each shows you something different.
kernels.l6: A finite set with n members has 2ⁿ subsets, by induction or by matching each subset with a yes-or-no answer at every member. That second view is where the alternative notation for the power set comes from.
kernels.l7: A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets, proved by induction with a case split on whether a chosen element is in or out. Matching each subset with one yes-or-no answer per element gives a second proof and explains the alternative notation for the power set.
kernels.l8: The finite count generalizes to Cantor’s theorem |P(S)| > |S| for every S, whose diagonal proof is not an induction and cannot be one.

kernel: A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets. The step: pick a ∈ S, split subsets into those containing a and those not; each group is in bijection with the subsets of the k-element set S \ {a}, giving 2ᵏ + 2ᵏ = 2^{k+1}.
